_purpose: Companion to taught_morphemes.json: the learned words and grammar focuses this cohort has been taught, by term and week. Read this instead of re-mining old week specs when planning review weeks, dictation (section 6 needs learned words from 2-3 weeks ago) and the taught-only question rule (section 2b gates grammar labels). The builder does not read this file.
_rule: Append a week's learned words and grammar focus when its specs are delivered. For Term 3, the unfair part and Say it line are the settled values - reuse them verbatim instead of re-deciding them. Record each week's Friday vote under reviews; it is the class-level signal for next week's From our reviews line (OG_MEGA_PROMPT 12). Morphemes live in taught_morphemes.json, and the words taught from each uncaptured card live on its morpheme_bank.json entry.

term3._source: Term 3 week specs og_planner/weeks/term3_week1-10.json. Week 10 reviewed all 18 words and taught none.
_corrections: tongue: Week 1 highlighted ongue, Week 2 highlighted ue. Settled on ongue - both the o saying /u/ and the silent ue are unfair.
asthma: Week 9 notes said AST-muh, but the t is not pronounced. Correct Australian pronunciation is AS-muh.

words.why: the c is silent, so sc just says /s/; you hear the c as /k/ in muscular
the o says /u/ and the ue is silent, so gue just says /g/
ough says /ow/ here, but /uff/ in enough and /oh/ in though
uoy says /oy/; English almost never puts those letters in that order
after the c, ui says a short /i/
ts says /s/ because the word kept its Japanese spelling
ou says /uh/ and the French -age says /ahzh/
ei says long /i/ (Greek seis); graph is the same ending as pictograph
ci says /sh/ and es says /eez/; one species, ten species
Greek ch says /k/ and the a says /uh/
the r is silent and the o says /uh/; you hear the r in ironic
eo says one short /e/ and ard says /uhd/
au says long /ay/ here, not the /or/ of caught
two u letters in a row, saying /yoo/ then /uh/
the l is silent
the l is silent, exactly like salmon
the th in the middle is silent
y is the only vowel letter and says a short /i/; the h behind the r is silent
busi is busy with its y changed to i; the u says /i/ as in busy and the i is silent
the c after the s is silent, as in science and scene; the a says /ah/ from Italian
French: the ending eur says /er/ and entre says /on-truh/; links to business (Week 1)
the p is silent; ei is fair (i before e except after c); the p is heard in reception
the b is silent - scribes added it to match the Latin debitum (owed); you hear it in debit
Australian spelling; the que says /k/ as in unique and antique (Americans write check)
the u after the g is silent, as in guard and guess
the t is silent and age says /ij/; Old French mort gage, dead pledge - mort as in mortal

term3._source: Term 3 week specs. class_language is the wording students met - reuse it in later review.

weeks.class_language: a preposition tells where, when or direction; the phrase includes its whole noun group

weeks.focus: Identify adverbials and switch them to the front and back
weeks.class_language: an adverbial tells when, where, how or why; a fronted adverbial takes a comma
comma only when the detail is at the front
a clause has its own verb, a phrase does not; a main clause stands alone, a subordinate clause leaves you waiting
an appositive renames the noun beside it, inside two commas; cover it and the sentence still works

weeks.focus: Differentiate between simple, compound and complex sentences
weeks.class_language: Sentence Smackdown signals - one finger stands alone, a fist leaves you waiting, two fingers compound; hand chop at the split

weeks.focus: Identify main and subordinate clauses and the subordinating conjunction
weeks.class_language: labels M, S and T; T is the trigger word; a fronted S takes a comma

weeks.focus: Use nominalisation for variety, objectivity and an impersonal tone
weeks.class_language: action word -> thing word; the person steps out; word bank -ence -ance -cy -ice -ity -acy

weeks.focus: Define acronym, recall common acronyms, use brackets to expand one
weeks.class_language: full name first, short form in round brackets, then the short form alone; initialisms treated as acronyms
Tue prepositional phrases + adverbials; Wed phrase, clause + appositive; Thu simple/compound/complex + trigger word; Fri nominalisation + acronyms (no Monday session)

term3.labels_used: preposition and noun group (Week 1), verb (from Week 4), subordinating conjunction (Weeks 6-7), noun and verb (Week 8). adjective and adverb were never taught as labels - keep them out of questions outside the grammar section (section 2b).

term4._source: Term 4 week specs. class_language is the wording students met - reuse it in later review.

weeks.class_language: three upgrades - exact (exactly who or what?), strength (does it fit the facts? too strong is hyperbole), built up into a noun group (describer, noun, detail); Mon exact, Tue strength, Wed noun group, Thu all three

three verb upgrades - exact (exactly what happens?), strength (does it fit the facts? too strong is hyperbole), saying verbs (how was it said? warn, insist, agree, admit, show); Mon exact, Tue strength, Wed saying verbs, Thu all three, Fri week review. First week on v1.6 rounds: I do, one We do item, three You do items, answer on the click

weeks.focus: Join sentences using connectives to link arguments, evidence and reasons
weeks.class_language: however and on the other hand = the other side, therefore = so, the result, for example = the proof; the connective starts the second sentence and takes a comma. First v1.7 week: one grammar block, Thursday only. Parts of speech on suffixes taught from this week: noun names it, verb does it, adjective describes a noun, adverb tells how, when or where.

weeks.focus: Identify the function of a semicolon and generate a compound sentence where a semicolon replaces the conjunction between two independent clauses
weeks.class_language: a semicolon joins two full sentences and takes the place of and, but or so - never both; test each side can stand alone; small letter after it unless I or a name. First v1.8 week: parts of speech read from a sentence - what job does the word do here? noun names a thing or idea, verb is something you do, adjective describes a noun (frames retired 23 Oct 2026, before it was taught).

term4.from_our_reviews: noun, verb or adjective; guarantee and mortgage
